title: Stop People-Pleasing: Shamanic Healer Anahata Ananda on Inner Healing
guestBio: Anahata Ananda is a Shamanic Healer, Master Teacher, Certified High-Performance Coach, and Soul Guide based in Sedona, Arizona. She is the founder of Shamangelic Healing and Shine, Sedona's Sanctuary for the Soul, and has spent over 25 years training with shamans, energy healers, and spiritual teachers across North America, Peru, India, and Asia. For more than 20 years she has trained Lightworkers and Healers in shamanic healing modalities and breathwork facilitation.
excerpt: Shamanic healer Anahata Ananda joins Aimee Rickabus to unpack the people-pleasing patterns women are conditioned into — and the inner child, breathwork, and boundary practices that break them. If you've ever shrunk yourself to keep the peace, this conversation was made for you.
metaDescription: Shamanic healer Anahata Ananda on breaking people-pleasing patterns, inner child reparenting, shamanic breathwork, and building unshakeable boundaries.
keyTakeaways: People-pleasing and overcompensating are two sides of the same wound — both are walls around the heart that keep women from accessing their authentic power.
Emotional release alone is not healing; true transformation requires replacing old patterns with new, compassionate frameworks through what Anahata calls 'Shamangelic' healing.
Your emotions are intelligent data, not liabilities — learning to treat them as a compass rather than something to apologize for is foundational to leadership.
Inner child reparenting is a concrete, visualizable practice that rewires the stories you've carried since childhood and allows you to show up differently in every area of life.
Every time you level up — whether through sobriety, a new boundary, or a career leap — your relationships will be tested, and that tension is a sign you are growing, not failing.
Shamanic breathwork reaches trauma stored in the body that talk therapy often cannot access, by using hyper-oxygenation to surface and release held memory.
Building intuition is a daily practice that starts small: when you consistently honor the whispers in low-stakes moments, you develop the trust you need for the biggest decisions of your life.

quiz.title: What's Your Inner Healing Edge Right Now?
quiz.description: This isn't a test — there are no wrong answers here. These six questions will help you discover where your most powerful growth edge lives right now, and which part of this conversation with Anahata Ananda is speaking directly to you.

A.name: The Quiet Fire
A.description: You have been playing small for so long that even you have forgotten how much heat you're carrying. You are deeply capable, deeply feeling, and deeply tired of making yourself palatable for people who have never had to shrink. The people-pleasing wasn't weakness — it was wisdom for a season that is now over. This episode will give you the language and the permission to begin the break-up with the version of you that survival built.

B.name: The Armored Achiever
B.description: You have built something impressive — and you built the armor right along with it. High performance is real, your results are real, but somewhere underneath the calendar and the credentials is a little girl who learned that doing more was safer than being seen. Anahata's work on overcompensation and inner child reparenting will land somewhere you didn't know needed landing. This episode is your invitation to put something down.

C.name: The Awakening Leader
C.description: You are mid-transformation — you can feel it. Old friendships are shifting, old patterns are surfacing, and you are starting to trust the quiet voice inside more than the loud voices outside. You are not falling apart; you are leveling up. This episode will validate everything you are sensing and give you a practical breathwork and intuition framework to anchor the next chapter of who you are becoming.

D.name: The Integrator
D.description: You have done the work — therapy, retreats, the books, the journaling — and yet something still feels like it hasn't fully clicked into place. You are not broken and you are not behind. You are ready for the layer underneath the layer. Anahata's integrated Shamangelic method and the specific mechanics of inner child reparenting will give you the missing piece that intellectual understanding alone never could.

questions.question: When you imagine speaking your full truth in a high-stakes moment — to your boss, your partner, your mother — your first instinct is:

options.text: To soften it, reframe it, make sure no one feels bad first.
To prepare so thoroughly that no one can argue with the data.
To say it, then immediately wonder if I said it wrong.
To say it clearly — but notice I'm still waiting for the other shoe to drop.

questions.question: When you think about your inner child — the little girl you once were — your gut reaction is:

options.text: Sadness. I feel like I let her down by learning to disappear.
Protectiveness. I built this whole life so she would never feel that way again.
Curiosity. I'm starting to understand how much she is still running things.
Readiness. I've met her before — I just want to go deeper this time.

questions.question: The last time you held a real boundary — said no, changed an agreement, or walked away — the response from people around you was:

options.text: Confusion or hurt, and I nearly caved to fix it.
They tested it repeatedly to see if I meant it.
Mixed — some respected it, some pulled away, and both felt important.
Fine on the outside, but I'm still processing whether I did it "right."

questions.question: When you feel a strong emotion during an important moment — a meeting, a conversation, a decision — your most honest response is:

options.text: I push it down immediately. Feelings at the wrong time cost me.
I redirect it into action. Doing something is easier than feeling something.
I let myself feel it and then wonder why I'm still apologizing for it.
I treat it as information — but I'm still learning to fully trust what it's telling me.

questions.question: When a close friendship shifted because you grew or changed, your honest experience was:

options.text: I shrank back to preserve the relationship. It wasn't worth losing her.
I kept moving and told myself I didn't need people who couldn't keep up.
It hurt more than I expected, and I'm still making peace with it.
I understood it intellectually but I'm still working on releasing the grief.

questions.question: When you try to access your intuition on a big decision, what's most honest?

options.text: I can't hear it. Everyone else's voice is louder than mine.
I hear it — and then I override it with logic and research.
I'm starting to hear it more, especially in small moments.
I hear it, but I second-guess it enough that I still hesitate to act.

content:
There is a version of you that learned, very early, that keeping the peace was safer than telling the truth. She smiled when she wanted to scream. She said yes when every cell in her body was saying no. She made herself smaller so the people around her could feel bigger. And she was so good at it that most people — maybe even you — called it kindness.

It wasn't kindness. It was survival. And in this episode, Aimee sits down with shamanic healer Anahata Ananda to talk about what it actually takes to break up with that version of yourself — and who you get to become on the other side.

Two Walls Around the Same Heart

Anahata has worked with women for over 25 years, and she says she sees the same two coping patterns playing out in almost every story she encounters. The first is playing small — shrinking, deferring, apologizing for taking up space. The second is overcompensating — hustling harder, controlling more, building an identity so armored that nothing can get through. These patterns look completely different on the outside. But Anahata is clear: they are both walls around the heart. Both are responses to the same original wound. And neither one is living.

What she describes isn't a character flaw. It's conditioning. Women are socialized from childhood to prioritize everyone else's comfort over their own inner truth. That programming runs deep — deeper than a mindset shift or a motivational quote can reach. Which is exactly why Anahata's work goes somewhere most personal development doesn't.

The Night She Chose Herself

Anahata doesn't just teach this work. She's lived it. She opens the episode with one of the most striking cold opens in recent Manage Her memory: "My integrity was not for sale. My relationship was not for sale." She was three years into a marriage. She had three-year-old twins at home. And she made a decision — not from fear, not from anger, but from what she calls absolute authentic power — that most people around her could not understand.

She calls it "marital liberation," and she says it with zero apology. Because the alternative — staying in a life that was suffocating her soul to avoid rocking the boat — was never actually an option for the woman she was becoming.

Why Emotional Release Is Not Enough

When traditional therapy didn't reach what needed reaching, Anahata found her way to a shamanic session for the first time, 27 years ago. She describes releasing "such a heaviness" — a kind of unburdening that talk therapy hadn't touched. But here's the nuance that makes her approach different from a lot of healing spaces: Anahata is emphatic that emotional release alone is not healing.

Crying it out, screaming into a pillow, hitting a mat — these things can move energy. But if you don't intentionally fill that space with something new — compassion, a new story, a reparented relationship with yourself — you will reach for the old patterns again. Her "Shamangelic" method is specifically designed around this: release first, then compassion, then integration. It's the difference between clearing a wound and actually healing it.

The Inner Child Is Not Metaphor

At the 29-minute mark, the conversation gets beautifully concrete. Anahata walks through the inner child reparenting visualization step by step — what it looks like, what it feels like, what you're actually doing when you close your eyes and go back for that little girl. This is not abstract spiritual language. It is a practice. A specific, repeatable intervention that rewires the stories you formed about your worth, your safety, and what you have to do to be loved.

She's made a free guided version available specifically for Manage Her listeners — you'll find the link below — and Aimee's reaction in real time is worth noting. This is a CEO and mother of six who runs a nine-figure company, and she is fully present, visibly moved, and already signed up for Anahata's apprenticeship starting in January. That should tell you something.

Your Emotions Are Not the Problem

One of the most quietly radical things Anahata says in this episode comes around the 33-minute mark: your emotions are intelligent. They are not inconvenient. They are not unprofessional. They are not something you need to manage into silence before you can sit at the table. They are a compass — and women who have spent decades apologizing for them have been navigating without one.

This reframe matters enormously for women in leadership, in marriage, in motherhood — anywhere you've been told that having feelings means you're too much, too sensitive, or not ready. Anahata invites you to stop pathologizing your emotional body and start consulting it.

Breathwork, Boundaries, and the Friendship Tax of Leveling Up

The conversation covers the mechanics of shamanic breathwork — how hyper-oxygenation allows the body to surface and release memories that live below the threshold of conscious recall, reaching what years of talk therapy sometimes cannot. And it gets honest about something most growth content glosses over: when you change, some people leave. When Anahata made the decision to get sober, friendships shifted. When she started holding real boundaries, the people who had benefited from her boundarylessness pushed back hard. She doesn't sugarcoat this. She calls it the friendship tax of leveling up — and she says the key is building an internal foundation strong enough that someone else's discomfort doesn't become your reason to collapse.

The One Practice That Builds Everything Else

If you take one thing from this episode, let it be this: start with the little things. Anahata's daily intuition practice isn't about waiting for a big download or a dramatic sign. It's about noticing the small nudges — the coffee shop you feel drawn to, the route that calls you, the name that pops into your head — and honoring them. Every time you do, you are building a track record of trust with yourself. And when the big decision lands — the one about the relationship, the company, the move, the dream — you will have the receipts to know you can be trusted to hear yourself clearly.

As Anahata says near the close of this conversation: "Big decisions aren't coming. They're here." The question is whether you've done the daily work to meet them with clarity instead of fear.

This episode is a gift. Listen to it twice.
